title_on_roster: Dorothy Foehr Huck and J. Lloyd Huck Chair in Neurorehabilitation Associate Professor

evidence.quote: Xiaogang Hu Dorothy Foehr Huck and J. Lloyd Huck Chair in Neurorehabilitation Associate Professor

research.text: We have a interdisciplinary group of researchers with engineering, science, and clinical background. Our research mission is to restore motor and sensory functions of individuals with neural or muscular injuries. Our research focuses on 1) the fundamental problems of control and neuromechanics of the arm and hand after neural or muscular injuries, and 2) the development of neural-machine interface techniques that can reduce sensorimotor deficits in clinical populations. We develop and implement interdisciplinary approaches in signal processing, machine learning, neuroscience, computational modeling, assistive robotics, and wearable sensing. Our long-term goal is to improve functional recovery and enhance the quality of life of disabled individuals, and maximize research translation to clinical practice.

research.text: Consisting of a large number of intricately connected neurons, the brain is one of the most sophisticated dynamical systems in nature. Understanding how the brain computes is at the forefront of current scientific research. Research in our group focuses on theoretical analysis of biological neural networks and computational models of song generation in songbirds, speech recognition in humans, and learning and memory in the hippocampus. The modeling is done in close collaboration with experimental groups.

research.text: Our research focuses on developing a new way to control gene activity inside cells with precision. Imagine being able to “switch on” specific genes in a safe, non-invasive manner, exactly when and where they are needed. To achieve this, we use focused ultrasound—a technique already widely applied in medicine—that gently warms targeted cells. This mild heat activates natural genetic switches in the cells, called heat shock promoters, which then trigger gene expression. In our study, we engineered human stem cells with a genetic system that permanently turns on a green fluorescent marker when activated by these promoters. We tested several promoters and found two, called HSP16F and synHSPB′3, to be especially effective.
